sense: what is in a container, a book or a letter

terms.gloss: what is in it, the contents
terms.grammar: phrase: a relative clause with īnsum (in with the ablative); plural quae īnsunt
evidence: Gell. 3.14.3: argentī … quod in eō scyphō inest
terms.comment: Latin says what is in a thing; it has no general noun for “contents”.

terms.gloss: the contents of a book, a letter or a play: its subject
evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. argūmentum: “contents, subject, theme”
terms.comment: Also, and first, a proof or an argument (see subject).

terms.gloss: the content, as against the words
terms.grammar: noun, fifth declension; opposed to verba
evidence: Cic. Or. 51: in philosophiā rēs spectātur, nōn verba penduntur (Lewis & Short)

terms.grammar: phrase: index, indicis m. with the genitive plural of caput
terms.comment: Classically index is a list or catalogue (Quint. 10.1.57) and the title of a book (Lewis & Short); the phrase is Traupman’s. Morgan-Owens gives rērum cōnspectus.

phrases.latin: argentī autem, quod in eō scyphō inest, dīmidium meum esse
phrases.english: but that half of the silver in that cup is mine

phrases.latin: In amōre haec omnia īnsunt vitia: injūriae, suspīciōnēs, inimīcitiae, indūtiae, bellum, pāx rūrsum.
phrases.english: in love there are all these faults: wrongs, suspicions, quarrels, truces, war, peace again

phrases.latin: in philosophiā rēs spectātur, nōn verba penduntur
phrases.english: in philosophy it is the content that counts; words are not weighed
